personas.role: Runs the resource server: prices routes, issues bound challenges, verifies credentials and returns receipts, usually through mppx middleware.
goals: Charge per call or per token without accounts or invoices
Accept stablecoins and cards from the same 402 response
Get paid before any side effect runs
pains: Managing the HMAC secret that every challenge id depends on
Choosing between charge and a session for streaming endpoints
Keeping up with SDK advisories and changelog fixes (five mppx advisories in 2026, the last fixed in 0.8.2)
implements: mppx server with one or more methods and a secretKey
Cache-Control no-store on 402 and private on receipts
mustTrust: The rail to settle what it confirms
Its SDK version to enforce replay and close rules
Discovery crawlers to list it accurately (advisory only)
questions: Which methods do my buyers actually hold?
Do I sponsor Tempo fees with feePayer or hostedFeePayer?
How do I refund a stablecoin charge if delivery fails?
firstSteps: Run the mppx server quick start on the Moderato testnet
Add a second method (stripe) to the same route and read both challenges
Run the latest mppx (0.14.1 on 2026-10-21) and watch both its advisories and its changelog, which lists security fixes without an advisory
personas.story: Priya sells a weather API by the call. Her route answers unpaid requests with a Tempo challenge and a Stripe challenge, both bound with the HMAC secret she rotated last week. Overnight an agent fleet pays 40,000 times at one cent each; the receipts carry transaction hashes she reconciles each morning. A partner wants to stream forecasts per minute, so she adds a session route and caps the suggested deposit. When an advisory about fee payer draining appears, she upgrades mppx, checks her fee wallet balance, and adds a daily ceiling. Her one open worry: refunds on stablecoin charges are her own policy.

personas.role: Builds the client or agent that receives challenges, decides whether to pay and produces credentials.
goals: Pay any MPP server on the first request
Keep keys and limits out of the model's reach
Support both MPP and x402 without two code paths
pains: Bearer credentials that anyone can spend if they leak
Tempo channels that never expire: they stay open until the server closes them or the client forces a close
Method support that differs by SDK
implements: mppx client wrapping fetch, with Accept-Payment preferences
Checks on amount, recipient, currency and expires before signing
Session bookkeeping: open, voucher, close, forced-close fallback
mustTrust: The server to deliver after payment
The rail to cap loss (deposit, SPT limits)
Its own policy hook to reject bad challenges
questions: How much can this agent lose in the worst case?
Which channels are still open and how do I close them?
What happens if the server never answers my close?
firstSteps: Run the mppx client quick start against the mpp.dev paid ping on testnet
Add a policy extension that rejects unknown recipients
List and close retained sessions with the mppx CLI
metrics: Open channel count and locked deposit
personas.story: Marco ships a research agent that buys search results and model tokens. He wires mppx into fetch and adds a policy hook that refuses any challenge whose recipient is not on an allowlist or whose amount exceeds two cents. For a model provider the agent opens a Tempo session with a five dollar deposit, so the worst case is five dollars. At the end of each task his code sends a close; a nightly job lists retained channels and force-closes any the server ignored, waiting the full grace period. He never logs credentials, because whoever copies one can spend it.

personas.role: Processes MPP charges on card and fiat rails: Stripe for the stripe method, or, in the card method written by Visa, a Server Enabler that decrypts the token and requests authorization from the card network (a Client Enabler provisions the token).
goals: Bring existing card and wallet acceptance to machine clients
Keep raw card data out of client and server scope
Reuse fraud, tax, refunds and reporting
pains: Mapping one challenge to one PaymentIntent or authorization
Unclear SPT cost allocation: Stripe's US pricing page lists 0.15 USD per SPT issued, listed since at least 2026-04-23, but does not name the party billed
implements: PaymentIntent creation with confirm true, an idempotency key from challenge id and SPT, and a check of Stripe's Idempotent-Replayed header
JWE decryption and network authorization as Server Enabler
Network token and cryptogram provisioning as Client Enabler
mustTrust: The merchant server to validate the challenge before charging
The card network for authorization and dispute rules
questions: Is this payment card-not-present with agent involvement, and how do disputes work?
What metadata ties a PaymentIntent to its challenge?
Does Stripe's listed 1.5 percent stablecoin rate apply to MPP charges?
firstSteps: Run the mppx stripe example in test mode
Map PaymentIntent and authorization references into receipts
personas.story: Lena works on acceptance at a payment processor that already serves Visa merchants. The card method, written by Visa, lets her team act as a Server Enabler: merchant servers forward an encrypted token they cannot read, her service decrypts it and asks the network for authorization. Chargebacks still follow card network rules, and Visa's rules now include agent-specific provisions. In the first week a merchant's buggy client sends the same credential twice; her idempotency checks return the first authorization instead of charging again. She reports authorization rates for agent traffic separately, because nobody yet knows whether it behaves like ordinary card-not-present volume.

personas.role: The software that pays: reads challenges, chooses a method within its limits, signs, retries and keeps receipts.
pains: Challenges that look valid but name the wrong recipient
implements: Pre-payment checks on amount, currency, recipient and expires
Receipt storage with reference and timestamp
mustTrust: Its operator's policy and key custody
questions: Is this price within my budget for this task?
Did I get a receipt for every paid response?
firstSteps: Read the challenge and decode request
Check amount, recipient, currency and expires against policy
Pay through the preferred method and store the receipt
personas.story: An overnight procurement agent needs ten datasets. For each it requests the file, receives a 402 with two challenges and decodes both. One is a Tempo charge for 0.40 USD to an address its operator approved; the other is a Stripe charge it is not configured to use, so it ignores it. It checks that the challenge expires in four minutes, signs and retries, and stores the receipt hash in its task log. One server asks for 40 USD with a reassuring description. The agent ignores the description, compares the amount with its budget, refuses, and flags the server for its operator.

personas.role: Builds an independent controls layer (budgets, allowlists, monitoring, kill switches) around MPP clients and servers.
goals: Enforce budgets the protocol does not have
See every payment an agent makes
Stop spending quickly when something goes wrong
pains: No protocol kill switch or revocation message
No native agent identity: only an optional payer id, optional TAP headers in the card method and mppx's request attestation
implements: Policy extensions that run before mppx signs
mustTrust: Rail-level limits such as SPT max_amount
questions: Where can I intercept a payment before it is signed?
How do I prove a payment to an auditor?
How long can a channel stay open unseen?
firstSteps: Add an mppx extension that enforces a per-task budget
Export receipts and channel states to a ledger
Alert on open channels older than a set age
personas.story: Sam runs the controls team for a company with 300 agents. MPP gives him clean hooks: every payment starts with a decoded challenge, and mppx runs his extension before it signs. His extension checks a per-agent budget, a recipient allowlist and a maximum price per unit for sessions. A dashboard joins stored receipts with on-chain settlements. The gap he cannot close in policy is time: Tempo channels never expire, so his nightly job force-closes channels idle for a day. When an agent misbehaves, he revokes its key at the wallet, because the protocol has no stop button.

rows.step: Issue the bound challenge (402 with WWW-Authenticate: Payment)
Check amount, recipient, currency and expires
Pay through the method (sign, mint SPT, get card token)
